title: New Mac Mini Has Two Storage Downsides, Including Unremovable SSD
content:
As confirmed by the website "Expand Mac mini," NAND storage in the new Mac mini models with the M6 and M5 Pro chips is soldered to the logic board, whereas the previous models with the M4 and M4 Pro chips have removable storage that can be upgraded.


In other words, the new Mac mini does not support aftermarket storage upgrades.

"Expand Mac mini" offers plug-and-play SSD modules that are functionally equivalent to Apple's proprietary modules, yet hundreds of dollars cheaper. As a result, customers were able to save a significant amount of money by configuring their Mac mini with the minimum 256GB capacity that was available on Apple's online store and later installing a higher-capacity aftermarket module. With the new models, that is no longer possible.

"We will keep looking for an opening, but support for the M6 and M5 Pro now looks unlikely," the "Expand Mac mini" website said, in a blog post.

Mac mini models with the M1 chip and M2/M2 Pro chips also had NAND soldered to the logic board, so the M4/M4 Pro configurations having removable storage has proven to be a one-off exception for now. Apple has not commented on the reversal.

AAPL Ch.'s testing with Blackmagic's Disk Speed Test benchmark tool.

The new 256GB model's Disk Speed Test scores were roughly half that of models with 512GB of storage or more. The average customer is unlikely to notice the difference, but power users will appreciate knowing that they need to opt for at least 512GB of storage in order to achieve the fastest SSD speeds possible.

Fortunately, even with 256GB of storage, it appears that the new Mac mini has meaningfully faster SSD speeds compared to the previous 256GB model.

title: OpenAI's New GPT-6 Sol and Luna Models Bring Astra Improvements to Cheaper Tiers
content:
OpenAI today launched GPT–6 Sol and GPT–6 Luna, two new models that follow GPT–6 Astra. OpenAI says the new models were developed using methods similar to Astra's for improvements in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment.


GPT–6 Sol is for everyday work, and it costs less than Astra. GPT–6 Luna is an even cheaper model. Luna is optimized for fast responses and higher volume, while Sol has more reasoning capability.

The new models outperform their predecessors on OpenAI's benchmark tests, and GPT–6 Sol makes "about half as many mistakes" as GPT–5.6 Sol. GPT–6 Sol shows improvements in coding and computer use compared to GPT–5.6 Sol, and it matches or beats Claude Fable 5.1 scores on some benchmarks.

Opus 5.5 model today that outperforms Astra on some coding and knowledge work benchmarks.

GPT–6 Sol and Luna are adopting the improved communication style OpenAI introduced with Astra for simplified conversations with less jargon and fewer low-value details. Answers should be slightly shorter without losing substance, and the new models have lower rates of misleading claims about their coding work in OpenAI's alignment testing.

OpenAI is lowering token prices for Sol and Luna compared to their 5.6 counterparts, and prompt caching has been improved. OpenAI says agents will reuse more context, respond faster, and get 90 percent discounts on cached input-token reads.

GPT–6 Sol is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, down by half. GPT–6 Luna costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, down from $0.20 and $1.20, respectively. GPT–6 Sol costs half as much per token as Opus 5.5, but Anthropic says Opus 5.5 uses fewer tokens per task than Opus 5, so it's not a straight comparison.

title: Apple’s new Beats headphones are AirPods Max for athletes
content:
Macworld





The newest Beats over-ear headphones are here, and as evidenced by the many leaks, are made for athletes. Specifically, athletes who liked the idea of AirPods Max but passed on them because they were too heavy, too drab, or, most importantly, too expensive.
First, the price: Beats 360 are $350, significantly less than the $449 AirPods Max. For that price, you’re getting much of what Apple’s high-end headphones offer: Active Noise Cancellation, Transparency mode, Personalized Spatial Audio with dynamic head tracking, and Adaptive EQ. iPhone users will also get one-touch pairing, Automatic Switching, Audio Sharing, Find My support, and hands-free “Hey Siri.”
While Beats says they have “the best acoustics from Beats to date, as well as the best noise cancellation yet from Beats,” they don’t have some features AirPods users might miss. Since they have a custom-designed proprietary Beats chip rather than an H2, you’re not getting AirPods features such as Live Translation, Hearing Protection, and Conversation Boost.
However, if you can live without those features, Beats 360 are everything AirPods Max aren’t. Most notably, they’re very light, weighing just 295 grams, versus AirPods Max’s 386 grams. The cushions are available in one of two options: performance knit for workouts or ultralush for longer listening sessions. They also come in a variety of bright colors–Black, Cloud (off-white), Pink, and Sky (blue)–that are encouraged to be mixed and matched with different cushions, which are available in their own set of colors and cost $50 each, with a special launch price of $10.
While AirPods Max aren’t rated for water resistance, Beats 360 have IPX4 sweat and water resistance, making them very gym friendly. They also feature on-device controls for controlling music. You get 32 hours of battery life, about 50 percent more than AirPods Max.
You can order Beats 360 on the Beats websites, or through Amazon and other third-party retailers for shipping beginning Thursday.
creator: Macworld

Opus 5.5 is comparable to Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, so Anthropic is launching it with safeguards similar to those on Fable 5.1. Opus 5.5 also generates output over 30 percent faster than Opus 5.

On benchmarks shared by Anthropic, Opus 5.5 surpassed Fable 5.1 on agentic coding, knowledge work, computer use, visual chart recognition, and multidisciplinary reasoning. Anthropic says the model communicates more naturally than prior models, putting important information at the front of a response so it's easier to understand at a glance. It is less likely to use jargon or idiosyncratic phrases, and it follows the writing rules it's given.

title: Amicus briefs show strong support of Apple's arguments ahead of Epic Supreme Court judgement
content:
While the US DOJ won't take sides in a case, the Solicitor General did file a brief sharing that violating "the spirit of the injunction" wasn't within standards, echoing Apple.


Apple is ready to face the Supreme Court in October
The Apple vs Epic lawsuit has been ongoing for over six years. It started as an intentional violation of Apple's App Store rules, which led to the lawsuit and almost total victory for Apple on all but one charge.
Apple was ordered to remove its anti-steering practices, which it did, but was found in violation of the injunction due to not following the spirit of the injunction. After more than a year of back and forth, the Supreme Court will soon weigh in on the matter, and various firms have filed amicus briefs ahead of the October decision.

title: How to clear System Data on Mac and free up storage space
content:
Macworld





If your Mac is warning that you are running out of storage, you need room for a macOS update, or your Mac simply seems to be slowing down, you may have looked at the large chunk of storage labelled System Data and wondered if you can safely delete it to save space on your Mac. 
Low storage can cause all kinds of problems on a Mac – you might see warnings that your startup disk is almost full, struggle to install macOS updates, notice performance slowdowns, or in extreme cases even have trouble starting up your Mac. Maintaining at least 10% of your total storage as free space is generally recommended to ensure your Mac continues to run smoothly.
So what exactly is System Data, why can it grow so large, and is it safe to remove anything from it? The answer is yes — at least some of it. Just beware that deleting some files from System Data could seriously damage your installation of macOS, so we recommend that you back up your Mac before deleting anything, just in case!
In this guide, we’ll explain what’s included in System Data, why it can take up so many gigabytes, and the simple steps you can take to delete System Data and reclaim space on your Mac. If you aren’t sure how to see how much disk space your Mac has read: How to check how much disk space you have.

You don’t need extra efforts to get the most of the disk space by checking hard drives, creating new partitions, allocating volumes and converting disk/partition format to read-write ExFAT. What’s more, it allows NTFS read/write so that you will use your Mac like daily operations under Windows. Now 25% OFF by using code: MACWORLD25.

What is System Data on Mac?
System Data on Mac is a broad storage category that serves as a catch-all for various files that do not fit into standard classifications like Applications, Documents, or Photos. 
While the specific contents vary for every user, System Data typically includes the following types of files:
Caches and Logs: System and application caches designed to help your Mac run more smoothly.
Temporary Files: Data created during daily use that is often intended to be deleted automatically by the OS.
Backups: Local Time Machine snapshots and iOS backups.
Plug-ins and Extensions: Support files for various applications.
Disk Images: Downloaded .dmg files used for upgrading apps or macOS.
App Leftovers: Bits of data that remain on the drive even after the main application has been deleted.
System Data, System, macOS and Other 

				
					

				
			
Find out what’s taking up all the space.

Foundry




Apple has changed how this storage category is labeled in different versions of macOS.   
In macOS Big Sur (macOS 11) and earlier, much of this storage was grouped under a category called “Other.” In macOS Catalina (macOS 10.15) and the subsequent Big Sur, there was also a separate category labeled “System,” which included core macOS files and other system-related data.

				
					

				
			Older versions of macOS labeled certain types of storage as System or Other. 
Starting with macOS Monterey (macOS 12), Apple reorganized these categories, replacing much of the System/Other terminology with “System Data,” while also introducing a separate “macOS” category for the operating system itself.
In newer versions of macOS, including Sequoia and Golden Gate, the category continues to appear as “System Data” alongside the separate “macOS” category.






Why is System Data so large? 

				
					

				
			
System Data was over 100GB. Is that a record? 

Foundry




System Data is intended to be managed automatically by macOS, but it can occasionally balloon to an unexpected size, sometimes taking up more than 100GB of storage. This is particularly problematic on Macs with smaller 256GB SSDs, where System Data can unexpectedly consume nearly half of the available space. 
This happened to us when macOS started temporarily storing update-related files inside System Data as well as reindexing iCloud and Spotlight files while preparing to install an update to macOS. That was when we concluded that a 256GB SSD is too small for a Mac.
System Data can grow as apps and macOS accumulate caches, logs, temporary files and other support data. The main cause varies from Mac to Mac.
Key factors that drive the growth of System Data include:
Streaming Caches: One of the biggest culprits is streaming high-quality music and video. While downloaded media is indexed separately, streamed content creates large caches to ensure smooth playback, which are categorized as System Data.
Browser and App Caches: Safari and other browsers store website data to speed up loading times. Over time, these caches can grow to several gigabytes.
Messaging Data: If you frequently send and receive high-resolution images or videos via apps like Messages, the cached attachments can significantly inflate system storage.
System Maintenance: Files such as Time Machine snapshots, iOS backups stored on a computer, and macOS update installers often reside in this category. 
The impact of local AI models on System Data
A new and increasingly common cause of large System Data storage is the rise of local artificial intelligence features. Modern operating systems, browsers, and apps now download sizeable AI models so they can perform tasks directly on your device rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.
These local AI models can have a significant impact on macOS storage because the model files themselves are often several gigabytes in size.
Features such as Apple Intelligence, offline transcription tools, coding assistants, and image-generation apps may all store large language models, caches, and other AI assets locally on your Mac. Many of these files are saved in hidden Library folders, caches, containers, or developer directories, so they don’t appear in obvious categories like Applications or Documents. Instead, they can dramatically increase the amount of storage attributed to System Data.
AI workloads can also create large temporary files, caches, and logs while models are running, further increasing storage usage over time.
Apple Intelligence adds to your Mac’s storage requirements. For macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple lists up to 14GB of on-device storage for Macs with M3 or later and at least 12GB of unified memory, and up to 8GB for other compatible Macs. These are storage requirements for Apple Intelligence – not an indication that all of that space will appear under System Data.






Is it safe to delete System Data on a Mac?

				
					

				
			Beware: Deleting is permanent.
Foundry




Apple does not provide a simple Delete button for System Data because the category contains many files required for macOS to function properly. If it were possible to remove everything included in System Data, it could seriously damage your installation of macOS.
However, some files classed as System Data are non-essential and can be safely removed to free up space. These may include certain caches, logs, temporary files, old backups, and unused application support files.
That said, you should proceed carefully and only delete files if you are confident you understand what they are. Removing the wrong files can lead to application errors, system instability, or, in extreme cases, prevent your Mac from starting up properly.
In particular, you should avoid deleting:
Operating System Files: Core macOS files required for the system to run.
System Caches: These help macOS and apps run efficiently, and deleting the wrong cache files can cause problems.
Hidden System Files: Apple hides many critical files specifically to prevent accidental damage.






What System Data files can I safely delete? 
If you need to free up storage space on your Mac, there are several types of System Data files that are generally safe to remove.
Old Time Machine Snapshots: Local Time Machine snapshots can sometimes consume large amounts of storage space. These are temporary backups stored on your Mac and can usually be safely deleted if you already have backups saved elsewhere.
iPhone and iPad backups: Old iOS and iPadOS backups stored on your Mac can take up many gigabytes. If you no longer need them, they can be safely removed.
Application caches: While you should avoid deleting core system caches, clearing caches created by individual apps is usually safe. Keep in mind that many apps will simply recreate these files over time.
Disk image files (.dmg): Downloaded installer files for apps you have already installed are often left behind in the Downloads folder and can safely be deleted once they are no longer needed.
Temporary files and logs: Some temporary files and log files generated by apps and macOS can be removed, especially if they are old or unusually large. However, proceed with caution, as some of these files are necessary for system performance and stability.
Unused AI model files: Modern versions of macOS and some third-party apps may download large AI models for on-device features. Don’t manually delete Apple Intelligence files from system folders. For third-party AI tools, remove unused models through the app’s own controls. 
We’ll explain how to manually remove files from each of these categories below. We’ll also recommend some apps that can help you with this. 






Best apps to delete System Data on a Mac
If you don’t feel confident deleting these files manually, you may prefer to use a dedicated cleanup tool to reduce the risk of accidentally damaging macOS or deleting important system files. 
There are several specialized cleaning utilities specifically designed to identify and remove System Data files including large caches, logs, and temporary files that are often difficult to locate manually. These tools can help identify potentially removable files, but review their recommendations before deleting anything. How to delete System Data on a Mac
If you feel confident deleting files manually rather than paying for a dedicated cleanup tool, here’s what you need to do to reduce the size of System Data on your Mac. 
Before you begin, there are a few things you should do: 
Empty the Trash: Files moved to Trash continue to occupy storage until you empty it. Review its contents first.
Restart your Mac: This can clear temporary caches and other system files that macOS no longer needs.
Back up your Mac: It’s recommended to back up your Mac before deleting anything categorized as System Data. Some files in this category are essential to macOS, and deleting the wrong files can cause instability, data loss, or even prevent your Mac from booting properly.





1.
Look for other data to delete first

				
					

				
			
Before you attack System Data check to see what else you can delete. 

Foundry






Before you start deleting System Data files, check whether there’s anything else you can safely remove first.
macOS includes built-in storage management tools that can help you identify large files and unnecessary clutter. In macOS Ventura and later, go to System Settings > General > Storage to see a breakdown of how your storage is being used.
Storage settings show how your Mac’s space is being used. Where a category has an information button, click it to see the available management options. System Data is a catch-all category and doesn’t have a single cleanup button.
For example, the Documents section highlights Large Files you may no longer need, while Messages provides quick access to images, videos, and attachments cluttering up the Messages app.
If Mail is storing attachments locally it could be using a huge amount of space. Review junk and deleted messages in Mail and use Mailbox > Erase Junk Mail and Mailbox > Erase Deleted Items to remove them. 
You’ll also see recommendations to help optimize storage, such as enabling iCloud Photos or automatically emptying the Trash.
If you would rather avoid deleting files altogether, another option is to move data to external storage or cloud services instead.
2.
Remove Time Machine Snapshots

				
					

				
			
EaseUS






Local snapshots normally don’t need to be deleted. macOS counts their space as available storage and automatically removes them as they age or when other tasks need the space.
If you need to remove local snapshots, temporarily disable automatic backups. Open System Settings > General > Time Machine > Options, change Backup Frequency to Manually, and click Done. Wait a few minutes, then restore your previous backup frequency.
If you use Apple’s Time Machine to back up your Mac, it may also create local snapshots on your Mac. These snapshots allow you to recover recently deleted files or restore earlier versions of documents even when your Time Machine drive is not connected.
Optional: Remove snapshots using Terminal
Local snapshots created by Time Machine can consume considerable disk space. macOS should automatically delete these snapshots when space is needed; however, if you want to remove them manually, you can do so using Terminal commands.
To see all local snapshots, open Terminal and enter:
tmutil listlocalsnapshots /
Note the date of any you want to delete and then paste in:  
sudo tmutil deletelocalsnapshots 2026-05-10-120102
Replace the date above with the snapshot date relevant to your case.
If you would prefer to remove multiple snapshots at once, you can enter the following command, which asks macOS to free approximately 10GB of snapshot storage:
sudo tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 10000000000 4
3.
Delete old iOS backups

				
					

				
			Find iOS backups in Manage Backups. 
Foundry






If you back up your iPhone or iPad to a computer rather than to iCloud, those backup files can quickly take up a significant amount of storage space.
Deleting old iOS backups is an effective way to reclaim storage space.
If you’re using macOS Catalina or later, follow these steps:
Connect your iPhone or iPad to your Mac.
Open Finder.
Select your device from the sidebar.
Under the General tab, click Manage Backups.
Select any outdated backups and click Delete Backup.
Before macOS Catalina, iOS backups were managed through the now-discontinued iTunes app.
4.
Clear Caches

				
					

				
			
Delete Caches from the Finder.

Foundry






Clearing caches on a Mac can help free up storage space and sometimes improve performance. In most cases, it is safe to delete cache files because they are recreated automatically when needed.
You can manually clear different types of caches through Finder.
Only remove cache files you can identify, preferably using the app’s own controls or its developer’s instructions. Don’t empty cache folders indiscriminately.
Delete User Caches: These are files created by your applications. To access them, open Finder > press Command+Shift+G > type ~/Library/Caches/. Use an app’s own cache-clearing controls where available. If a particular app is using excessive storage, quit it and follow its developer’s instructions for removing its cache. Avoid indiscriminately emptying Library folders: they can contain data you still need. Applications will rebuild caches automatically when needed, but the rebuilt caches may quickly consume the space again. 
Delete Browser Caches: Safari, Firefox, and other browsers store cached website data that can sometimes cause slow loading or display issues. You can clear data directly within their settings to speed up sluggish web browsing. See our article on Deleting Browser Caches for details. 
Restart: Restarting your Mac or quitting apps that have been running for a long time can automatically clear some temporary cache files and recover system resources.
Use Safe Mode: Starting your Mac in Safe Mode automatically clears certain system caches, which can temporarily free up storage. On a Mac with Apple silicon, shut down, then hold the power button until startup options appear. Select your startup disk, hold Shift, and click Continue in Safe Mode. On an Intel Mac, start or restart while holding Shift until the login window appears. After logging in, restart normally to leave Safe Mode. macOS recreates these caches as needed, so the space saving may be temporary.
We also have a guide to how to clear cache on a Mac. 
5.
Delete Disk Images 

				
					

				
			
Search for DMG files in the Finder. 

Foundry






Typically, when you install software on a Mac using a disk image, the .dmg file remains in your Downloads folder (or wherever it was originally saved).
Even after you drag the application into your Applications folder, the .dmg file remains on your Mac until you delete it manually.
The mounted disk image itself – the volume that appears on your Desktop or in Finder – is usually ejected automatically when you restart, log out, or manually eject it. However, the original .dmg file still remains on disk.
These files can contribute to the storage categorized as System Data or Documents until they are deleted.
To locate these files: 
Open Finder
Use the search bar and search for files ending in .dmg or .pkg
These files can usually be safely deleted after installation if you no longer need them for reinstalling software later.
6.
Remove Xcode files

				
					

				
			
Xcode 26

André Martin






If you have ever installed Xcode there may be many related files on your Mac filling up System Data. Xcode is known for consuming a significant amount of storage on a Mac. 
While the initial download is substantial, the total disk space used often increases over time as you download additional components, such as iOS or watchOS simulators, and accumulate derived data from building projects.
To reclaim storage being used by Xcode follow these steps: 
Quit Xcode. 
Open the Finder. 
Click on Go > Go to Folder. 
Enter ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData, and review its contents before moving them to Trash.  
Another option is the following Terminal command to delete Xcode’s DerivedData folder, which contains generated build data. It does not remove downloaded simulator runtimes or every file associated with Xcode. Subsequent builds will need to regenerate this data.
rm -rf ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData
7.
Wipe your Mac and reinstall

				
					

				
			
Foundry






If none of the above have helped reduce the size of your System Data, the nuclear option is to do a clean install.
Consider erasing your Mac only if you have a persistent storage problem that you cannot resolve through targeted cleanup. Before proceeding, verify your backup and identify how you will restore documents, photo libraries, email stored locally, and app-specific data. Some important information lives in Library folders, so don’t exclude all Library data without checking what your apps need.
This will require you to completely wipe your Mac, so make sure you have a backup first. However, if you restore a full system migration from a Time Machine backup, you may also restore whatever caused System Data to become overloaded in the first place. 
Reinstalling macOS without erasing the disk preserves your apps and data, so it won’t necessarily resolve excessive storage use.
For help performing a clean install, read our dedicated guide here: How to clean install macOS on your Mac.
You can also reduce the amount of wasted storage on your device by following the tips in how to free up space on Mac. For more advice read our tips for cleaning up your Mac to make it run faster.

title: Apple Watch Series 10 vs. Series 12 Buyer's Guide: Should You Upgrade?
content:
The Apple Watch Series 12 is now available, two years after the Series 10 introduced the current thinner design. But is it worth upgrading?


While last year's Series 11 brought just four changes, the Series 12 is a much more substantial update, with a new chip, twice as much RAM, redesigned health sensors, exclusive health and audio features, tougher cover glass, 5G connectivity, and new case materials.

The Series 12 starts at the same $399 price as the Series 10 did in 2024. Apple has now discontinued the Series 10, but remaining units may still be available from third-party retailers and on the refurbished or second-hand market. Here are all of the key hardware and feature differences between the Apple Watch Series 10 and Apple Watch Series 12:

Up to 38 hours in Low Power Mode

15 minutes of charging for up to 12 hours of normal use

Five minutes of charging for up to 10 hours of sleep tracking

Design and Display

The Series 12 retains the same basic design introduced by the Series 10, including 42mm and 46mm size options and a 9.7mm-thick case. Nevertheless, Apple has made some subtle dimensional changes. Both sizes are now 1mm wider, and every equivalent aluminum or titanium configuration is between 2.1 and 3.3 grams heavier than its Series 10 counterpart.

shrunk slightly. Resolution is unchanged, but the active display area is around 2% smaller on both sizes. The combination of a wider, receded case and smaller display produces thicker borders around the screen.

Is It Worth Upgrading?

Two generations on, the Series 12 represents a meaningful cumulative upgrade over the Series 10, but it is far from an essential replacement. The two models share the same basic design, display brightness, resolution, storage capacity, core safety features, and more. The Series 10 is only two years old, and supports watchOS 27 and ‌Siri‌ AI, so it remains a capable and modern Apple Watch.

For existing Series 10 owners, upgrading is easiest to justify if health and fitness tracking is a priority. The Series 12's high-frequency heart rate sensing, Recovery HRV, daytime vitals, Readiness score, and improved step tracking provide substantially more useful training and recovery data. Sound Recognition may be compelling for deaf or hard of hearing users, while 5G, faster charging, tougher cover glass on aluminum models, and the ceramic case provide additional reasons for some buyers to upgrade.

Beyond this, the practical difference between the two devices is relatively small. The Series 12 is also slightly wider and heavier, and its active display area is around 2% smaller despite retaining the same resolution. Its 24-hour battery rating is also not directly comparable with the Series 10's 18-hour figure because Apple changed its testing methodology. If your Series 10 still comfortably lasts through the day and you are satisfied with its existing health features, there is no strong general-purpose reason to replace it.

Which to Buy Today?

At its $399 starting price, the Series 12 is the obvious choice over a Series 10 selling for anything close to its original price. The newer model offers a better health sensing system, twice as much RAM, the S11 chip, exclusive Audio Intelligence features, faster charging, 5G, and more case options. A saving of only $50 to $100 is unlikely to compensate for giving up those improvements.

title: Apple Event This October? These 7 New Products Expected Next Month
content:
As usual, September has been a very busy month for Apple, with the company unveiling the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, AirPods 5, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4, Beats 360, and more. Nevertheless, Apple reportedly still has many more products to release later this year, including a new iPad mini, Apple TV, HomePod mini, iMac, and more.


It seems quite likely that Apple will hold an October event this year to announce at least some of the rumored new products, while others might be introduced in press releases. Below, we have recapped what to expect from Apple next month.

Apple does unveil new products in November or December sometimes, but this is less common.

What


iPad mini: A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip, an OLED display, a new speaker system without holes, and a water-resistant design.
 
24" iMac: M6 chip and new color options.

14" and 16" MacBook Pro models with OLED displays: A major MacBook Pro redesign in late 2026 with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, an OLED display, a touch screen, a Dynamic Island, and a thinner design.

Apple TV: At least five new features, including an A17 Pro chip or newer, an increased 8GB of RAM for Apple Intelligence, Siri AI support, an Apple-designed N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, and an updated Siri Remote. The new Apple TV will apparently look similar to the existing model, so do not expect any major design changes.

HomePod mini: Newer chip with Siri AI support, improved sound quality, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 support, a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, and potentially new color options like red. The new HomePod mini will apparently look similar to the existing model, so do not expect any major design changes.

Home Hub: An all-new Apple smart home hub featuring Siri AI, a 6-inch to 7-inch square display, an A18 chip or newer for Apple Intelligence, FaceTime, and more. A new operating system will feature clock faces, widgets, and more. There will be a tabletop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version.

title: iPhone 18 Pro & Max Guide: Everything you need to know about the new iPhones
content:
Macworld





The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are now on sale. They retain the 6.3-inch and 6.9-inch screen sizes and aluminum unibody design introduced with the previous generation, but Apple has made substantial changes to the cameras, processor, cooling, battery life and connectivity.
The biggest camera upgrade is a new 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture, which can automatically move between ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8 and ƒ/4 depending on lighting and depth of field. The widest aperture lets in more light for low-light photography, while new Pro controls let users manually adjust aperture, shutter speed and white balance, and view a histogram to assess exposure.
Inside is the A20 Pro, Apple’s first iPhone chip made using a 2nm process. It has a new six-core CPU, seven-core GPU, Dual 16-core Neural Engine and 50% more memory bandwidth than the A19 Pro. A larger vapor chamber and new M-series-inspired chip packaging also improve heat dissipation, with Apple claiming up to 40% better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro.
Other major changes include up to 36 hours of Apple-rated video playback on the Pro and 45 hours on the Pro Max on eSIM-only models, faster wired charging, and a redesigned Dynamic Island capable of showing three Live Activities simultaneously. The smaller iPhone 18 Pro also introduces Apple’s C2 cellular modem (Apple’s documentation doesn’t make it clear if this features in the Pro Max). 
iPhone 18 Pro/Max vs iPhone 17 Pro/Max: Top 10 changes at a glance

				
					

				
			iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17 Pro
Foundry




The five biggest changes are the variable-aperture camera, A20 Pro, improved cooling, longer battery life and redesigned Dynamic Island/connectivity system. Here is an overview of what’s new compared to the previous generation.  


FeatureiPhone 18 Pro / Pro MaxiPhone 17 Pro / Pro MaxWhat’s changed

Main camera48MP, variable ƒ/1.48–ƒ/4 aperture48MP, fixed apertureMajor new photographic control
ProcessorA20 Pro, 2nmA19 ProNew manufacturing process
GPU7-core, up to 40% faster6-coreSignificant graphics boost
Neural EngineDual 16-core / 32 cores total16-coreAround 2x AI compute
CoolingVapor chamber with 3x surface areaFirst-gen vapor chamberUp to 40% better sustained performance
Pro Max battery45 hours video39 hours+6 hours
Pro batteryUp to 36 hours video on eSIM model33 hoursUp to +3 hours
Wired charging50% in around 15 minutes50% in around 20 minutesFaster charging
ModemApple C2 (in Pro, unconfirmed in Pro Max)Qualcomm modemPro switches to an Apple-designed modem
Dynamic IslandRedesigned, 3 Live ActivitiesPrevious design, up to 2More information displayed simultaneously

 



Apple has added a 2TB option to the smaller Pro for the first time, while retaining 256GB as the entry-level capacity.


iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: Release date and availability 
The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max were announced on Wednesday, September 9, 2026. They started shipping from Friday, September 18, 2026 in more than 65 countries and regions and in another 20 countries from September 25.
You can buy the phones directly from Apple online or at Apple Stores, as well as through mobile networks and authorized Apple retailers. Apple sells unlocked iPhones directly through its website and stores.
Buy iPhone 18 Pro and Max at Apple U.S. 
Buy iPhone 18 Pro and Max at Apple U.K. 
$1199 at  Apple						
					
$1299 at  Apple						
					






iPhone 18 Pro/Max design: What does it look like?

				
					

				
			
This is the Burgundy variant (we think Deep Cherry was a much nicer name).

Foundry




The iPhone 18 Pro retains the aluminum unibody introduced with the iPhone 17 Pro, as well as the Ceramic Shield on the rear and Ceramic Shield 2 over the display. The camera system remains arranged on the large raised plateau across the upper part of the rear casing.
Screen sizes are unchanged at 6.3 inches for the iPhone 18 Pro and 6.9 inches for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, both using Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz.
Apple offers four finishes this year:
Burgundy 
Glacier
Silver
Black
That means Cosmic Orange and Deep Blue disappear, while black returns to the Pro line despite pre-launch reports suggesting it would not. Read more about the color choices here: Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro colors.
The pre-event leaks suggested the basic chassis dimensions would remain very close to the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max, with the camera plateau rather than the body itself becoming thicker. We can confirm from our own research that the newer camera bump is approximately 0.5mm taller. This means that cases designed for the iPhone 17 Pro may not fit the iPhone 18 Pro. Before buying a case, check compatibility and  read our Best iPhone 18 Pro cases buying guide.
The new iPhones share the same screen sizes and overall form as their predecessors, but both models are slightly heavier this time. 
iPhone 18 Pro dimensions: 150 x 71.9 x 8.75mm / 5.91 x 2.83 x 0.34 in
iPhone 18 Pro weight: 7.44 ounces / 211 grams (17 Pro was 7.27 ounces / 206 grams with eSIM)
iPhone 18 Pro Max dimensions: 163.4 x 78 x 8.75mm / 6.43 x 3.07 x 0.34 in
iPhone 18 Pro Max weight: 8.78 ounces / 249 grams (17 Pro Max was 8.22 ounces / 233 grams with eSIM)
Changes to the Dynamic Island
Apple has redesigned the Dynamic Island. Apple says new display technology creates additional usable space and allows the Dynamic Island to display up to three Live Activities at once, for example navigation, music and a sports score.
Apple has not announced fully under-display Face ID. Pre-launch reports suggested that one or more infrared Face ID components could move beneath the OLED panel, allowing the notch to shrink, but Apple hasn’t confirmed the underlying sensor arrangement.






iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max cameras: Are the cameras the same?

				
					

				
			
The iPhone 18 Pro cameras.

Apple




Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have the same three-camera rear system. The main change is not resolution—all three remain 48MP—but the new variable-aperture Main camera and new computational imaging pipeline.
The three most notable camera upgrades are:
Variable aperture on the 48MP Main camera.
A new Main camera sensor and imaging pipeline, improving low-light performance and detail.
More extensive manual Pro controls, including aperture, shutter speed, white balance and histogram.





Rear cameras


CameraResolutionFocal lengthAperturePixel information
Fusion Main48MP sensor; 12MP at 2x optical-quality zoom24mm / 48mm, 1x / 2xƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8, ƒ/4 variable2.44μm quad-pixel / 1.22μm individual
Fusion Ultra Wide48MP13mm, 0.5x / macroƒ/2.21.4μm quad-pixel / 0.7μm individual
Fusion Telephoto48MP sensor; 12MP at 8x optical-quality zoom100mm / 200mm, 4x / 8xƒ/2.81.4μm quad-pixel / 0.7μm individual

 



The 2x and 8x optical-quality options use crops from the Main and Telephoto sensors respectively, producing 12MP images rather than 48MP captures.
The Main camera’s six-blade mechanical aperture can automatically open to ƒ/1.48 in low light or close as far as ƒ/4 for increased depth of field. Photographers can also select aperture manually.
Both Pro models also offer up to 8x optical-quality zoom from the Telephoto camera. Contrary to some earlier rumors, the variable-aperture camera is not exclusive to the Pro Max.


Photography and editing improvements
Computational photography: Apple has introduced a new imaging pipeline, smart focus tracking, improved Clean Up, Spatial Reframing, an Extend tool and Photographic Styles 3, which adds texture and grain adjustments.
Apple Reference Image (U.S. and U.K.): Will use signed data from the iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera sensor to create an unalterable reference image through Private Cloud Compute. Viewed alongside the edited photo in Photos, it helps users assess what has changed, providing a useful authenticity check for photographers, journalists and anyone sharing images. It’s off by default, to enable it go to: Settings > Camera > Reference Image > Add Reference Mode.
Front camera
Apple has retained the 18MP Center Stage front camera, rather than moving to the rumored 24MP sensor. It supports automatic reframing, Center Stage, ultra-stabilized video and Dual Capture.
The front camera remains visibly associated with the Dynamic Island. Apple has not announced an under-display selfie camera on the iPhone 18 Pro.
iPhone 18 Pro video changes
Frame rates: Cinematic effects can now be applied after shooting to ordinary videos captured at up to 60fps. The phones continue to offer 4K 120fps Dolby Vision for high-frame-rate shooting.
Time-lapse: Time-lapse receives a significant upgrade to 4K with Dolby Vision HDR.






A20 Pro processor: How fast is it?

				
					

				
			
Apple has redesigned the iPhone chip. 

Apple




Both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max use Apple’s new A20 Pro processor.
It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, down from the 3nm-class process used for A19 Pro, giving Apple more scope to improve efficiency and transistor density.
The chip includes:
6-core CPU
7-core GPU
Neural Accelerators integrated into the CPU/GPU architecture
Dual 16-core Neural Engine, 32 cores in total
50% more memory bandwidth than A19 Pro
Apple says the GPU is up to 40% faster than A19 Pro, while the Neural Engine offers roughly double the AI processing capability.
One particularly important change is the packaging. Inspired by Apple’s M-series Mac chips, A20 Pro places the processor die side-by-side with memory rather than stacking memory directly in the chip’s thermal path. This improves heat transfer and allows the processor to couple more directly to the vapor chamber.
That vapor chamber itself has three times the surface area of the iPhone 17 Pro’s system. Apple claims the combination delivers up to 40% better sustained performance, which should be most noticeable during gaming, video work and intensive on-device AI rather than ordinary web browsing and messaging.






RAM: How much memory does the iPhone 18 Pro/Max have?
Apple does not officially publish RAM capacities for iPhones. However, iFixit lists 12GB of LPDDR5X memory for both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, matching the reported 12GB in the previous Pro generation.
The main memory upgrade is bandwidth: Apple says the A20 Pro offers 50% more memory bandwidth than A19 Pro. This increases the amount of data its CPU, GPU and Neural Engine can transfer to and from memory each second.
Higher memory bandwidth can help accelerate demanding tasks, including on-device AI. Combined with the redesigned chip packaging and improved cooling, it should help sustain performance during intensive workloads. However, this does not necessarily mean that more Apple Intelligence or Siri AI tasks run locally rather than in the cloud..






iPhone 18 Pro/Max connectivity options 
C2 modem
The iPhone 18 Pro introduces Apple’s C2 cellular modem, replacing the Qualcomm modem used in the previous Pro generation. 
Apple says C2 delivers faster uploads while consuming 15% less energy than C1X, alongside AI-powered improvements to connection quality and reliability and support for mmWave in the U.S.
Apple’s technical specifications list C2 for the iPhone 18 Pro but do not identify the modem in the Pro Max.
Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
Like the predecessors, the 2026 iPhones use Apple’s N1 wireless networking chip, supporting:
Wi-Fi 7
Bluetooth 6
Thread
Satellite
Emergency SOS via satellite, Messages via satellite, Roadside Assistance via satellite and Find My satellite functionality continue. Apple made no announcements about full satellite internet or ordinary 5G data delivered by satellite, despite pre-launch rumors suggesting such a capability could appear.






iPhone 18 Pro/Max Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s changed?
Battery life is one of the most significant improvements.
Apple says eSIM-only models gain additional battery capacity because the space previously occupied by the physical SIM tray can be used for battery cells. Physical-SIM variants provide around two hours less video playback than equivalent eSIM-only models.
Battery-life improvements come from larger batteries and greater power efficiency, including the new 2nm A20 Pro processor.





iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max battery capacity and life
The table below compares battery capacity and Apple’s video-playback ratings for the physical-SIM and eSIM-only versions of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.


ModelSIM versionBattery capacityEnergyVideo playbackEquivalent iPhone 17 model: video playbackImprovement

iPhone 18 ProPhysical SIM4,056mAh15.86WhUp to 34 hours17 Pro: up to 31 hours+3 hours
iPhone 18 ProeSIM-only4,288mAh16.76WhUp to 36 hours17 Pro: up to 33 hours+3 hours
iPhone 18 Pro MaxPhysical SIM5,391mAh21.06WhUp to 43 hours17 Pro Max: up to 37 hours+6 hours
iPhone 18 Pro MaxeSIM-only5,567mAh21.75WhUp to 45 hours17 Pro Max: up to 39 hours+6 hours

 



We discuss the battery life for different iPhones in more depth separately. 


Wired charging
Wired charging is faster. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max can reach 50% charge in around 15 minutes when using a USB-C cable and a 60W-capable or higher power adapter that supports Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS). The adapter is sold separately. This compares with around 20 minutes for the iPhone 17 Pro generation. Apple also says five minutes of wired charging can provide around seven hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro Max.
MagSafe and wireless charging
Apple says both models can reach 50% charge in around 30 minutes using a MagSafe Charger paired with a 35W or higher power adapter, both sold separately. MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging support up to 25W. Wireless charging speeds are broadly unchanged from the iPhone 17 Pro generation.






iPhone 18 Pro software: iOS 27 and Siri AI 
The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max support Siri AI in iOS 27, but the upgraded assistant isn’t enabled automatically. 
To request access, open Settings > Siri, enable Siri if necessary, then tap Try Siri AI (Beta). 
Then follow the setup instructions to join Apple’s waiting list. 
Access may arrive within minutes, hours or days, with a notification when it’s ready. 
Your device and Siri languages must both be English, and availability depends on your Apple Account region. You may also need up to 14GB of free storage. See how to get Siri AI for setup instructions and details of regional restrictions.






iPhone 18 Pro problems: What owners are reporting
Some iPhone 18 Pro owners have reported screens that intermittently stop responding to touch. Others report freezes and restarts after failed Face ID authentication, affecting both the Pro and Pro Max.
Macworld has not independently confirmed these problems, although multiple customers have described similar experiences. It remains unclear whether the issues stem from hardware or software. One owner said Apple support ran diagnostics and concluded their handset was faulty.
At the time of our report, Apple had not publicly acknowledged either issue or announced a fix. Read our report on iPhone 18 Pro freezes and restarts for the full details.





iPhone 18 Pro price: How much does it cost?
Apple has increased prices by $100 in the U.S. and £100 in the U.K. 
The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. Both begin with 256GB of storage.


ModeliPhone 18 starting priceiPhone 17 starting priceChange
iPhone Pro$1,199/£1,199$1,099/£1,099+$100/£100
iPhone Pro Max$1,299/£1,299$1,199/£1,199+$100/£100

 



Apple offers both models with 256GB, 512GB, 1TB and 2TB. That means the entry-level storage remains 256GB rather than increasing again. The notable change is that 2TB is now available on both models; previously the iPhone 17 Pro topped out at 1TB while the Pro Max could be configured with 2TB.
The $100 increase is considerably smaller than some analyst predictions before launch. Those forecasts had pointed to sharply higher DRAM and NAND costs caused by the global memory shortage, with estimates that the cost of 12GB of DRAM alone could rise dramatically this year. That makes component and memory pricing a credible contributor to Apple’s increase, although Apple itself hasn’t attributed the higher price to any one component.


Should you buy the iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max? Which model should you choose?

				
					

				
			
Which one do you want?

Apple




The iPhone 18 Pro is the better-value Pro model for most buyers, offering the same cameras and A20 Pro processor as the Pro Max in a more manageable 6.3-inch design. Choose the Pro Max if its 6.9-inch display and longer battery life justify the extra $100/£100 and additional weight. Apple rates it for up to 45 hours of video playback on eSIM-only models, or 43 hours on physical-SIM versions.
However, you may not need a Pro iPhone at all. Our best iPhone guide recommends the standard iPhone 17 for most people: its ProMotion display, dual 48MP cameras and 256GB of storage cover everyday needs for considerably less. Paying extra for the 18 Pro makes most sense if you want its dedicated Telephoto camera, variable aperture or additional performance for demanding games and creative work.
iPhone 17 Pro owners don’t need to rush to upgrade. Consider whether the variable-aperture Main camera, A20 Pro, improved cooling, faster charging and longer battery life will make enough difference to justify the expense. If your current phone comfortably handles everything you do, keeping it is a sensible choice.
For iPhone 14 Pro owners and earlier, the accumulated improvements make a stronger case. You gain USB-C, Apple Intelligence compatibility, higher-resolution Ultra Wide and Telephoto cameras, an improved front camera, larger displays and slimmer bezels. These changes span several generations: USB-C and the Action button arrived before Camera Control and the larger Pro displays, while the 18MP Center Stage front camera was already available on the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple Intelligence also supports the iPhone 15 Pro and later compatible models. This year’s variable aperture, A20 Pro and further battery improvements build on those earlier upgrades. Read why the iPhone 18 Pro rewards those who waited.
The iPhone Duo is worth considering if screen space and multitasking matter more than camera versatility. Its folding display and Split View offer something the Pro models cannot, but its $1,999/£1,999 starting price is $800/£800 above the smaller Pro. Despite that premium, it lacks a dedicated Telephoto camera and variable aperture. Choose the Duo for its folding design; choose a Pro for photography and better value. Our iPhone buying guide compares the specifications.
Both Pro models are now on sale, making this a good point in their release cycle to buy. If saving money matters more than upgrading immediately, Black Friday may bring better trade-in or carrier offers, although large outright discounts are unlikely so soon after launch. A substantially discounted iPhone 17 Pro is another option. See the best time to buy an iPhone.






Did Apple launch the iPhone 18?
There was no new iPhone 18 at the event. We expect the iPhone 18 to launch alongside the iPhone 18e and iPhone Air 2 in spring 2027. Read more about the iPhone 18 here: iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e: Release date, rumored specs and more.

title: If you bought a new iPhone in the past two years, Apple owes you money
content:
Macworld





iOS 27 has finally delivered on the new Siri promise Apple made back in 2024, but many people who were persuaded to buy an iPhone 16 at the time by ads touting the feature still feel cheated that it took so long. If you’re one of them, you can collect a check from Apple for your troubles.
Back in May, Apple agreed to pay $250m to settle a class-action lawsuit over deceptive marketing related to the debut of Apple Intelligence in 2024. Plaintiffs argued that Apple’s ads led to people buying iPhones back then that didn’t deliver on its promises and Apple settled rather than take the issue to court.
As a result, anyone who bought an iPhone 16, iPhone 16e, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 15 Pro, or iPhone 15 Pro in the U.S. between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025, is eligible for a cash payment of at least $25 per device with a maximum payment of $95 per device. As is usual with class-action payouts, the allotment “may be increased or decreased pro rata depending on the total number of valid claims submitted and Eligible Devices claimed.”
You may have already received an email about the settlement, which includes a Claim ID and PIN for filing. If you haven’t received one, you may still file a claim, but you’ll need your original iPhone’s serial number.
Payments won’t be distributed before February 24, 2027, when the Final Approval hearing will be held.

title: Brighter, lower-power iPhone OLED screens now delayed to 2029

Apple could move to newer OLED technology by 2029
The improved technology is called Color Filter on Encapsulation (CoE) OLED, and key to it is that it is OLED without a polarizing layer. That layer prevents blurring on screen, but there are significant benefits if it can be dispensed with.
Apple had previously been reported to be planning to use this screen technology in its 20th anniversary iPhone, due in September 2027. However, according to UBI Research, Apple will not use CoE until its Pro model iPhones in late 2029.

title: Beats 360 Deliver Customizability and a Revamped Over-Ear Headphone Design
content:
After months of teases and leaks, Beats is officially announcing its new Beats 360 headphone today. Priced at $349.99, Beats 360 represents a rethinking of the Beats over-ear headphone design, with an emphasis on sound quality, comfort, and customizability.

Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos.

Beats 360 is not a replacement for the brand's Studio Pro over-ear headphone, as the Studio Pro will remain part of the Beats lineup at a reduced price point of $299.99, down from the previous $349.99. Compared to Studio Pro, Beats 360 features a completely new acoustic architecture that delivers up to 1.75× more active noise cancellation and a 12dB increase in output while maintaining clarity across all frequencies with low distortion.

In addition to active noise cancellation (ANC), which utilizes a system of eight microphones to analyze the acoustic environment inside and outside the headphone, Beats 360 also support Transparency mode to still allow you to hear the world around you, while turning off ANC and Transparency activates Adaptive EQ to continually tune acoustic performance.



Personalized Spatial Audio with dynamic head tracking is also supported, allowing users to take full advantage of Apple's platforms that deliver 360-degree Dolby Atmos sound and move within the sound field as they turn their heads.
"Beats didn't just participate in the rise of over-ear headphones—we helped define the category," said Oliver Schusser, Apple's vice president of Music, Sports, and Beats. "Beats 360 is the next chapter of that story. We combined our most advanced acoustic performance ever with a perfectly balanced design that moves effortlessly with you. And with our new interchangeable cushions, our customers can express themselves in a way no other over-ear headphone can."
Beats 360 is available in four color options: Black, Cloud (an off-white), Pink, and Sky (a light blue). It includes comfortable color-matched Perfomance Knit ear and headband cushions, but the cushions are removable and interchangeable, allowing you to customize your favorite look and even change color combinations to suit the moment. Separate Performance Knit cushion kits are available in all four of the standard colors, plus Volt (a neon yellow-green) and Navy.


The Performance Knit memory foam cushions are breathable and ideal for working out and other active uses, but for the times you might prefer a more traditional cushion style, Beats is also introducing UltraPlush cushion kits in Black and Ivory. Similar to the ones found on Studio Pro and Solo 4, Beats 360 UltraPlush cushions feature a more pillowy feel with memory foam wrapped in engineered leather. Sensors in Beats 360 identify whether you are using Performance Knit or UltraPlush cushions, and they automatically adjust the acoustic tuning and noise cancellation filtering to maintain a consistent listening experience regardless of cushion material.

Beats 360 in dozens of color combinations

Cushion kits for both Performance Knit and UltraPlush will be priced at $49.99, but for a limited time and in select markets (US, UK, Canada, Australia, France, China, and South Korea), Beats is offering a launch promo that drops cushion kit pricing to just $9.99 or the rough equivalent in the local currency. Swapping out cushions is as simple as a quick twist on each ear cushion to remove and install, while the headband cushion snaps off and on with a small amount of effort while remaining securely attached during use.

Beats 360 in Sky

For active users, Beats 360 is the first Beats over-ear headphone product to feature an IPX4 sweat and water resistance rating, meaning it is protected against liquid ingress.

Beats 360 in Sky with Navy cushions

The removable cushions also make it easy to clean them, a welcome feature for those who plan to use Beats 360 for workouts. Beats recommends mixing one teaspoon (5ml) of laundry detergent into one cup (250ml) of water, rubbing the solution onto each cushion with a lint-free cloth for one minute each, wiping them clean with a separate cloth dampened with fresh water, and drying them with another lint-free cloth.



While over-ear and on-ear headphones have generally required thick headbands in order to accommodate multiple cables to connect the two ear cups, Beats 360 actually consists of two independent wireless earphones, with each containing its own battery, antenna and processing circuitry.

As a result, the headband houses only a single power cable to connect the two sides, allowing the batteries in both sides to be charged simultaneously from a single USB-C port. The thin headband also helps to optimize weight distribution, so while Beats 360 and Studio Pro are similar in weight at a little under 300 grams, Beats 360 puts more of the mass into the cushions where it matters most for comfort.

Siri" support is also included.


When it comes to battery life, Beats 360 deliver 32 hours of playback with ANC on, with a five-minute Fast Fuel charge giving you an hour of playback time in a pinch.

iCloud pairing and switching, Audio Sharing to allow a friend with compatible AirPods or Beats to listen to your audio, and Find My support. Android users get many of the same features with one-touch and ecosystem pairing, Audio Switch, and Find Hub geolocation.

Unlike the Beats Studio Pro, Beats 360 headband does not fold for travel, but the earcups do twist flat, and the headphones slide into a woven ripstop carrying case with a magnetic closure and a rear loop to hook onto a finger or carabiner. The case measures about 9 inches square and a little over 2 inches thick at its pleated bottom with the headphone inside. I prefer this flatter style of case to that of the Studio Pro, as it allows the headphone to fit into a computer bag or backpack more easily.

Cases for Beats Studio Pro (left) and Beats 360 (right)

In support of the 360 launch, Beats is debuting a new ad campaign featuring Kendall Jenner, led by a short film of Jenner meeting a friend at a cafe but realizing that everyone in the room is a different version of herself styled with a unique combination of ear cushions, emphasizing the individuality that's possible with Beats 360.


"I'm always on the go and switching between so many different looks," said Kendall Jenner. "So Beats 360 fits my lifestyle. I love that I can switch the cushions to match whatever I'm doing that day."

In a brief interview with Schusser at a Beats preview event earlier this month, he discussed how Jenner was an ideal candidate to promote Beats 360 given the many roles she plays throughout any given day in her personal and professional life.

He also addressed how Beats has been able to flourish under Apple's ownership, with Beats gaining access to all of Apple's expertise in audio as Apple and Beats engineers work side-by-side on products. At the same time, Beats has been able to maintain its own identity on the product design and marketing sides, continuing to focus on active lifestyle and celebrity marketing that remains distinct from how Apple promotes its own products.

available to order starting today at apple.com in the United States and more than 100 other countries and regions, as well as at Amazon and other third-party retailers. Availability follows this Thursday, September 24. It comes with the woven ripstop carrying case, while additional cushion kits, USB-C charging cables, and power adapters are sold separately.

title: New Mac mini does not have a slotted SSD, Mac Studio still does
content:
Two years after the M4 Mac mini released with an upgradable SSD, but Apple has changed course with the soldered new model. But, the new Mac Studio still has a slotted SSD with serialized components, so an upgrade there is at least possible.


Getting to the SSD storage module in a new Mac Studio - image credit: Apple.
Apple always used to solder its Mac storage in place, making it a permanent and so unchangeable, unrepairable feature. Given that Apple charges more for SSD storage than seems imaginable, it was big news when the last generation of Mac Studio and Mac mini changed this.
The M4 Mac mini came with a slotted, removable SSD, as did the M1 and M2 models of the Mac Studio. It's not as if Apple recommended upgrading your SSD yourself, but it was no longer making it impossible, and many people took great advantage. AppleInsider's Mike Wuerthele did it with an M4 Mac mini and then monitored it for six months, never finding any issues at all.

title: Apple’s next-gen photo controls only work on images ‘captured’ on a new iPhone
content:
Macworld





One of the more interesting elements of this month’s Surprise and Shine launch event was Apple’s subtle blurring of the boundary between hardware and software upgrades.
Many of the new health and audio AI features showcased for the Apple Watch Series 12, for instance, felt more like changes Apple would normally discuss in the context of the watchOS update at WWDC. Customers were naturally curious to know what new features they would be able to enjoy on older hardware, and Apple didn’t exactly rush to clarify the situation.
It does now appear, however, that one compatibility pledge has been reversed. Apple initially claimed that new texture and grain controls in the Camera app would be available for anyone with an iPhone 16 or later, provided they update their handset to iOS 27. But as spotted by the Twitter/X user CID, the same page now indicates that these features are exclusive to photos taken with the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo.


HOLYYY Apple just pulled the biggest SWITCHEROO after 10 DAYS
It seems they will no longer support older iPhones with the new photographic styles i posted this morning pic.twitter.com/08LktWDq2V
— CID (@theonecid) September 22, 2026





“The new texture and grain controls in Photographic Styles will be available on iOS 27 on iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro…” begins the quoted text in what the poster claims is its original form before an update on September 11. Whereas after the update the same section indicates that the new controls “will be available for photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro models and… iPhone Duo.”
I haven’t been able to find exactly the same wording but I can confirm the change as indicated in a separate document.
At time of writing, Apple’s press release for the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max contains an endnote (4) about compatibility: “The new texture and grain controls will be available for photos captured on iPhone 18 Pro models and the Ultra Wide, Main, and Center Stage cameras on iPhone Duo.”

				
					

				
			
Apple




When I use the Wayback Machine to view an archived version of the same page from September 10, the wording of this note changes drastically: “The new texture and grain controls will be available in iOS 27 on iPhone models that support the latest generation of Photographic Styles. See supported models.” Those last two words are a link to this list which clearly, even now, includes those older handsets.

				
					

				
			As you can see, note 4 has changed significantly.
David Price / Foundry




Indeed Apple appears to have decoupled latest-gen Photographic Styles, a general feature which is still something offered on iPhone 16 and later, from the specific subset of texture and grain controls. These latter features now have a separate compatibility list, and this only contains the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and Duo. However, that list pertains to the phones’ camera rather than the specific Photographic Styles tools. 
I contacted Apple to seek official confirmation of the change and to ask why this has happened. In a background statement, Apple reiterated the footnote saying photos need to be “captured” on one of the newest iPhones to use the new photographic styles but indicated that older phones will have access to the same editing tools for photos taken with an iPhone 18 Pro or Duo.
So it appears photos need to be taken by one of the newer phones in order to apply the new styles, but the tools themselves will technically be available on the older phones originally listed. Theoretically, you’ll be able to take a photo with a new phone and AirDrop it to an iPhone 17 for editing.
It’s unclear why they would be restricted to the newer phones, since the iPhone Duo essentially has the same camera as the iPhone 17 and 17e. In its press release for the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple says the new A20 Pro processor “features a new Dual 16-core Neural Engine, which accelerates on-device AI models and computational photography,” so it could be related to the new chip, which is only available on those three phones.

title: Apple Planning to Bring iPhone Duo Display Tech to Pro in 2029
content:
Apple's 2029 "Pro" iPhones could adopt thinner and more power-efficient OLED screens, according to UBI Research.


The technology, known as Color Filter on Encapsulation (CoE), removes the conventional polarizer from the ‌OLED‌ panel and places a color filter directly on top of its encapsulation layer. A polarizer helps suppress reflections from ambient light, but it also absorbs a significant portion of the light produced by the display.

Removing the polarizer allows more light to pass through, potentially enabling a display to reach greater brightness without consuming additional power, or use less power while maintaining the same brightness. Eliminating the separate layer can also make the display assembly thinner, freeing up internal space for components such as the battery, cameras, and more.

Samsung's internal testing, its original implementation improved light transmission by 33% and reduced power consumption by up to 25% compared with an ‌OLED‌ panel using a traditional polarizer.

CoE technology presents some technical challenges. Without a polarizer, manufacturers have to control external reflections through a combination of color filters, black pixel-defining layers, low-reflection coatings, and other optical measures. UBI Research believes the difficulty of maintaining outdoor visibility, viewing angles, contrast, and color accuracy may explain why Apple is reportedly waiting until 2029 to bring the technology to its high-volume conventional iPhone models.

iPhone Duo, reports indicated that its Samsung-supplied folding ‌OLED‌ display would use CoE technology. Apple has not detailed the panel's internal construction, but UBI Research sees the foldable device as a potential first step toward using polarizer-free ‌OLED‌ displays across the iPhone "Pro" lineup.

The research firm estimates that annual panel demand for the two Pro models could remain between 90 million and 100 million units, making the proposed transition significantly larger in scale than CoE's use in foldable devices. Samsung Display and LG Display are expected to lead the initial supply, while BOE could compete for orders if it can meet Apple's requirements.

title: Mac Studio 2026: M5 Max and M5 Ultra specs, prices and benchmarks
content:
Macworld






New Mac Studio 2026: At a glance
What’s new: The 2026 Mac Studio gains M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips, dramatically faster AI and graphics performance, faster SSD storage, increased memory bandwidth, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and enhanced professional connectivity. 
Release date: Announced on August 25, 2026
On sale: Shipping from September 22, 2026, but the Mac Studio with 512GB of unified memory is coming in late October.
Price: From $2,499/£2,499
In August 2026, Apple launched a new Mac Studio to replace the M4 Max and M3 Ultra model introduced 17 months previously. The 2026 Mac Studio retains its familiar compact design, but our testing reveals substantial improvements inside – particularly in SSD speed and graphics performance.
The previous generation mixed chip generations, pairing M4 Max with M3 Ultra. The new models bring both tiers into the M5 family: M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU and up to a 40-core GPU, while M5 Ultra scales to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Both feature Neural Accelerators built into every GPU core to boost AI processing.
Our M5 Max Mac Studio review found approximately 23 percent higher multicore performance in Geekbench 7 and 33 percent higher GPU rendering performance in Cinebench 2024 compared with the tested M4 Max Studio. Storage delivered the biggest leap: our 4TB configuration achieved approximately 2.7 times the read throughput and 2.2 times the write throughput. Results vary by workload, however, with our video export and encoding tests showing more modest improvements.
For M5 Ultra, Apple claims up to 1.3 times the CPU performance, 1.8 times the graphics performance and 4.3 times the AI compute performance of M3 Ultra, depending on the workload and configuration.


When is the new Mac Studio available?
The new Mac Studio with M5 Max and M5 Ultra was announced on August 25, 2026. Shipping of most configurations began on September 22. Apple has confirmed that Mac Studio models configured with 512GB of unified memory will ship in “late October.”
You can order the new Mac Studio from Apple, but you may find it discounted elsewhere. 
$2,499 at  Amazon										 | 
																$2499 at  Apple						
					
$5499 at  Apple						
					





How much does the new Mac Studio cost?


ModelPrice from
M5 Max, 36GB, 512GB$2,499 / £2,499 
M5 Ultra, 96GB, 1TB$5,499 / £5,499 

 



Higher-priced configurations include an M5 Max with a 40-core GPU and up to 128GB of unified memory, or an M5 Ultra with an 80-core GPU and up to 512GB of unified memory. 
Has the Mac Studio price gone up?
In June 2026, Apple raised the starting price of the Mac Studio by $500, from $1,999 to $2,499. The M3 Ultra model saw an even steeper increase, rising $1,300 from its $3,999 launch price to $5,299. The hikes were part of broader increases across the Mac lineup, which Apple attributed to sharply higher component costs, particularly RAM.
The new M5 Max Mac Studio remains at the June price of $2,499, but the M5 Ultra model has risen by another $200 to $5,499. That makes it $1,500 more expensive than the previous-generation Ultra model was when it launched in March 2025.
Here’s a breakdown of the key price changes for the Mac Studio:


ModelOriginal PriceJune Price M5 Update price
M4 Max, 36GB, 512GB$1,999 / £2,099$2,499 / £2,499$2,499 / £2,499 
M3 Ultra, 96GB, 1TB$3,999 / £4,199 $5,299 / £5,299$5,499 / £5,499 

 



When it comes to high prices, the M5 Ultra Mac Studio is filling the gap left by the removal of the Mac Pro from the line up back in March 2026.


Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra specs

				
					

				
			
Petter Ahrnstedt




Mac Studio moves to M5 Max and M5 Ultra, with up to a 36-core CPU, 80-core GPU, 512GB unified memory and 1.2TB/s memory bandwidth. Storage now uses PCIe Gen 6 for twice the performance, while connectivity adds Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and USB-C genlock. 
Processor: M5 Ultra and M5 Max chip compared
The Mac Studio comes with either Apple’s Max or Ultra chips. The Max chip is aimed at demanding professional and creative workflows and supports large amounts of unified memory and high memory bandwidth. The Max chip is also available as an option for the MacBook Pro. 
The Ultra chip combines two Max chips on one large chip using Apple’s UltraFusion architecture, so they offer double the CPU and GPU resources, and even higher memory capacity and bandwidth. It’s suited to complex 3D rendering, large AI models and scientific computing. 
M5 Max: We are already familiar with the M5 Max from the MacBook Pro that launched in March 2026. It offers an 18-core CPU and up to 40-core GPU, versus up to 16 CPU cores in the M4 Max. Its GPU includes a Neural Accelerator in every core, helping deliver up to 3.9x faster AI performance than M4 Max, according to Apple, alongside third-generation ray tracing. 
M5 Ultra: The M5 Ultra is a brand new chip that connects two dual-die M5 Max chips using UltraFusion, creating a four-die architecture and offerering up to a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. Apple claims up to 1.3x faster CPU, to 40% faster graphics and 4.5× peak GPU compute for AI versus M3 Ultra.





Mac Studio M5 Max benchmarks
We have tested the Mac Studio M5 Max with 18-core CPU, 40-core GPU, 128GB memory and 4TB SSD, here are the benchmarks for that model. Read our full review of the Mac Studio (M5 Max).


TestM5 Max StudioM4 Max StudioImprovement

Geekbench 7 single-core3,7823,5028%
Geekbench 7 multicore35,65829,06723%
Cinebench 2024 GPU22,43816,86633%
iMovie 4K ProRes export28 seconds31 seconds10% less time

 






Storage 
Maximum storage remains 8TB for the M5 Max and 16TB for the M5 Ultra, so capacity hasn’t increased.
However, Apple says its next-generation SSD architecture, based on PCIe Gen 6, delivers up to twice the storage performance.
Our testing of the M5 Max Mac Studio with a 4TB SSD showed substantial improvements over the tested M4 Max Studio:
2.67× the read throughput.
2.18× the write throughput.
These results apply to the tested configurations; performance may vary with SSD capacity. Faster storage could reduce the time spent opening large projects, transferring files and loading large local AI models, although the improvement will depend on your workload and any other bottlenecks. 






RAM
Maximum unified memory remains 128GB with M5 Max and 512GB with M5 Ultra, the same as the previous generation. 
Bandwidth has improved though. The M5 Max will now reach 614GB/s with the 40-core GPU configuration, up from 546GB/s on the 40-core GPU M4 Max, while M5 Ultra delivers 1.2TB/s, which Apple says is around 50 percent higher than M3 Ultra.






Connectivity: WiFi & Bluetooth
Other upgrades include Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, USB-C genlock and Thunderbolt 5 clustering for distributed AI workloads. Display support also improves, with M5 Max supporting up to five external displays and M5 Ultra supporting up to eight, depending on resolution and refresh rate.

				
					

				
			
Eugen Wegmann




Wi-Fi: The Mac Studio now supports Wi-Fi 7 which replaces the previous wireless standard Wi-Fi 6E.
Bluetooth: Bluetooth 6 replaces Bluetooth 5.3.
Ethernet: Existing connectivity including 10Gb Ethernet, HDMI, USB-A, SDXC and a headphone jack remains.
Thunderbolt: Thunderbolt 5 remains, offering up to 120Gb/s and as many as six Thunderbolt 5 ports depending on configuration. Thunderbolt 5 can now be used with RDMA to cluster multiple Mac Studios for distributed AI workloads; Apple says four systems can deliver up to 3x faster AI inference than one. 
Genlock: Apple has added Genlock support over USB-C. This is used for synchronising a display and camera (which can be an iPhone 17 Pro) and will be useful for professional video workflows.
Display support: The Mac Studio with M5 Max supports up to five external displays. The M5 Ultra supports up to eight displays at 6K/60Hz, or up to four displays at 5K/120Hz.
Other ports include two USB-C ports and an SDXC card slot on the front of the M5 Max model, and two Thunderbolt 5 ports and an SDXC card slot on the front of the M5 Ultra model. On the back of the Mac Studio are:
4× Thunderbolt 5 ports
2× USB-A ports
1× HDMI port
1× 10Gb Ethernet port
1× 3.5mm headphone jack

Who is the Mac Studio best for?
Apple has designed the Mac Studio with M5 Max to meet the needs of demanding creative and technical professionals. Apple specifically highlights musicians, photographers, software developers, designers and 3D professionals. It’s also well suited to video editing, code compilation, AI image generation and running sizeable LLMs locally.
The Mac Studio with M5 Ultra is intended for professionals with exceptionally demanding workloads: VFX artists rendering complex scenes, filmmakers working with multiple streams of 8K video, engineers running simulations, and AI researchers or data scientists training and running huge models locally. Its 512GB memory ceiling is particularly valuable for frontier-class LLMs.






Should you buy the 2026 Mac Studio?
For new buyers, the M5 Max Mac Studio is an excellent starting point. Pay extra for M5 Ultra only if your workload needs its additional resources.
Existing M4 Max owners should weigh an upgrade carefully. Our video tests showed relatively modest time savings, although workflows limited by internal storage speed may benefit more substantially. 
M3 Ultra owners shouldn’t assume M5 Max is faster across the board: it wins Cinebench GPU rendering, but M3 Ultra retains advantages in multicore rendering and Metal compute. Upgrade only if the benefits justify the cost for your work.
Availability may become limited due to the global RAM shortages. For more guidance, read: Should you buy a Mac Studio now or wait?
